title: When Is History Long Enough? Conditional Quantile Models versus Historical Rules for Peak Net-Position Limits

changes.before: Hard to Beat: Historical Rules versus Conditional Quantile Models for Peak Net-Position Limits
changes.after: When Is History Long Enough? Conditional Quantile Models versus Historical Rules for Peak Net-Position Limits

changes.before: Risk limits on dealer positions concern the largest magnitude reached before a review horizon ends, rather than the position at its endpoint. We compare historical and conditional quantile forecasts of sampled absolute-position peaks for an FX market maker and weekly primary-dealer position aggregates. Simple historical rules prove difficult to beat. At the shorter horizon, long-history FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% in the previously reported later and earlier windows. Its later advantage survives a delayed adaptive coverage adjustment (ACI). Before correction, however, regression breaches more frequently, while its ranking against a shorter-history rolling rule changes across periods. After stronger regularization, regression still loses 34 of 48 additional-panel comparisons. We formalize the known-floor target and apply a classical endpoint-to-peak bound under explicit assumptions. The results support joint validation of accuracy, breach behavior, and stability across reference rules, periods, and related series. A controlled simulation rejects a universal narrow-regime explanation, while aggregation and the overlapping backcast further qualify the empirical pattern.
changes.after: Peak-position limits concern the largest absolute inventory reached before a review ends, making completed path labels and the observed current position central to forecasting. We compare historical and conditional quantile reports for an FX market maker and weekly primary-dealer position aggregates, using matched histories and update schedules. Simple historical rules remain demanding benchmarks across frequencies, position categories and reference choices. At the shorter horizon, long-history FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% in the previously reported later and earlier windows. A post hoc history-to-horizon coordinate organizes simulation gains, and a new simulation passes its short-history and long-history prediction screens. Real-record learning curves partly support the predicted first cutpoints, while left censoring, large-history reversals and failures of universal simplification qualify that pattern. For limit managers, these findings motivate matching historical information before assessing conditional forecasts jointly on score, breaches and stability, with history length guiding evaluation.

changes.before: A dealer's recorded net position can finish inside its limit after exceeding it earlier in the monitoring period, as Figure~\ref{fig:example} illustrates. The forecasting question concerns the largest sampled exposure before the next review, rather than the endpoint alone. This changes the response and when its training label becomes available. We ask whether additional conditioning improves that peak forecast once historical information is matched, and whether the gain survives alternative references and breach assessment.
changes.after: An inventory limit can look adequate at the horizon endpoint even when a dealer's position has crossed it earlier in the review period. Figure~\ref{fig:example} shows why the relevant forecast is a sampled path maximum rather than an endpoint interval. The challenge is to learn that peak from completed historical labels while preserving the information available when the position is observed. We ask when additional conditioning improves on historical headroom forecasts that use the same training history, and how longer histories alter that comparison.

We examine these competing effects through matched histories, alternative reference rules, and repeated chronological comparisons.

Training-history length provides an organizing question for the comparisons, with the proposed explanation tested rather than imposed on every favorable and adverse result. A post hoc coordinate comparison motivates predictions for a new simulation grid and fixed-period FX learning curves under unchanged validation and evaluation clocks. The resulting support is partial: the broad simulated loss pattern survives, while universal simplification fails and the financial curves show censoring and reversals. This evidence guides history-sensitivity validation without identifying a unique estimation-cost channel or a permanent sample-size threshold.

changes.before: Quantile estimation and evaluation supply established tools for comparing conditional peak forecasts against historical rules on a shared response. Regression quantiles directly target asymmetric forecast errors through the associated loss function, providing the basic statistical building block \citep{koenker1978}. Conditional autoregressive quantiles and quantile forests provide additional conditioning structures for different forecasting applications \citep{engle2004,meinshausen2006}. Consistent scoring rules and elementary-score representations explain why rankings can vary across distinct evaluation questions \citep{gneiting2011,ehm2016}. We connect these tools to mature path labels, matched historical controls, and the stability of observed score and breach differences. Table~\ref{tab:literature} shows how the peak response, mature training labels and matched reference rules distinguish the present forecasting comparison.
changes.after: Quantile estimation and evaluation supply established tools for comparing conditional peak forecasts against historical rules on a shared response. Regression quantiles target asymmetric forecast errors, providing the basic statistical building block for the proposed conditional reports \citep{koenker1978}. Conditional autoregressive quantiles and quantile forests offer additional structures, while consistent scores explain why rankings depend on the evaluation question \citep{engle2004,meinshausen2006}. Learning-curve research documents diverse and sometimes nonmonotone relationships between training size and predictive performance across methods and data conditions \citep{viering2023}. Our fixed-period curves compare relative loss against a historical reference that also changes with training history, differing from an independent-sample expected-risk curve. Table~\ref{tab:literature} locates the peak response, mature labels and matched reference design, alongside the scoring tools discussed by \citet{gneiting2011,ehm2016}.

The history-coordinate comparison is a post hoc discovery on an existing simulation grid. We recorded the subsequent simulation equations, random streams, classification criteria and financial crossing predictions before running their new calculations, with local design commits and chronology available in the repository. This is a pre-run specification within an already examined research program, not a public external registration or an untouched financial holdout. The new simulations change innovation laws and random streams, whereas the FX learning curve reuses the known validation and evaluation period.

Every history shares the original validation segment and evaluation start, with complete mature-label pools and the original update convention; unavailable cases would remain NA. Both W2880 cases exactly reproduced all available old scientific arrays, summary fields and parameter selections before other histories were attempted. Some older parsimonious trace fields were absent, so their unavailable historical comparisons remain outside that claim. The bootstrap holds the selected coordinate fixed when resampling repetition clusters; its endpoint envelope conditions on that choice and the discovery grid. The new paired-loss diagnostics use the original Bartlett HAC convention with a normal reference and no family adjustment, treating financial dependence conditions as working premises.

A practical history screen is to examine the entire matched-loss curve around the available history and verify its breach behavior and temporal stability. The coordinate and its cutpoints can organize that investigation, but left censoring and later reversals require testing the actual reporting configuration. Treat a favorable region as a candidate for further validation rather than a permanent minimum-sample rule or an empirically measured sample-per-parameter threshold.

changes.before: A winning score leaves breach behavior and operating suitability to be assessed.
changes.after: The map guides history-sensitivity checks alongside breach behavior and operating suitability.

The history coordinate is descriptive, with parameter count absent from the selected index and dependence beyond the response horizon left unmeasured. Different penalty menus and approximation errors move together with predictor count, so the comparison does not isolate an estimation-cost channel. The new simulation's specified loss-pattern screens are met, while universal simplification fails and the financial grid supplies partial first-cutpoint consistency. Wide post hoc endpoint envelopes and left censoring limit threshold precision, while the longest-history reversals contradict a permanent operating cutoff. Weekly grids lack a dedicated broad-history learning curve, and some exceed the smaller model's point cutpoint without uniformly winning.

changes.before: Simple historical rules are strong competitors for predicting the largest sampled absolute position before a monitoring horizon ends. The original long-history FX regression gains against matched headroom survive in the broader backcast on previously examined observations, although score reductions coexist with more breaches. Longer-horizon backcast gains and the daily exception prevent a literal short-horizon or hourly-only interpretation. The controlled simulation also rejects the proposed narrow-regime restriction, while the same-dealer aggregation contrast leaves frequency mixed with measurement and clock changes. The defensible result is reference-sensitive comparative accuracy in these records, rather than a universal mechanism or validated operating-limit rule.
changes.after: Historical rules remain demanding competitors for sampled peak-position quantiles, with conditional gains depending on the reference, training history and forecast horizon. The post hoc history-to-horizon coordinate organizes the original simulations, and the new simulation grid supports its specified short-history and long-history loss patterns. Retrospective FX curves provide partial first-cutpoint consistency, while left censoring, long-history reversals and failed universal simplification qualify a single-threshold interpretation. The controlled study's earlier narrow-regime explanation still fails, so the history pattern adds a bounded organizing description rather than replacing contrary evidence. These results motivate validation at the actual history and reference, combining score, breach frequency and stability before a limit manager adopts additional conditioning.

changes.before: This revision adds three design-frozen exploratory extensions: a controlled simulation, a same-dealer daily aggregation contrast and an expanded inspected backcast.
changes.after: The earlier controlled grid, same-dealer daily contrast and overlapping backcast remain complete. This revision adds the post hoc coordinate comparison, pre-run simulation screen and fixed-period financial learning curve, with all counterexamples and unavailable prediction statuses visible.
